For thirty-one years my grandfather repaired watches in a narrow shop between a bakery and a shoe store. The sign above the door said only "Repairs," because, he told me once, anything with a spring and a gear would eventually find its way to him anyway.

The week he closed the shop, he asked me to help him pack. I expected the job to take an afternoon. It took five long days, because every drawer we opened held something he wanted to explain. There was a pocket watch that had belonged to a train conductor, its case dented where it had struck a rail. There was a box of tiny screws sorted by a system only he understood, each compartment labeled in pencil with a number that had faded almost to nothing.

On the third day a woman came in with a wristwatch wrapped in a handkerchief. She had seen the sign in the window announcing the closing and hoped he might look at it one last time. My grandfather set down the box he was holding, pulled his stool to the bench, and fitted the loupe to his eye. For twenty minutes the only sound in the shop was the faint click of his tweezers against metal. When he handed the watch back, it was ticking. He refused to take her money.

After she left, he sat for a while without speaking. Then he picked up the box again and went on packing.

On the last evening, after the shelves were bare, he unscrewed the old sign from above the door and carried it to the car. It sits now in my hallway, a little crooked on its nail. Sometimes, when the house is quiet, I find myself listening for a ticking that belongs to a room that is gone.

Dead satellites, spent rocket stages, flecks of paint, and fragments from collisions now circle the Earth by the millions. Most pieces are smaller than a marble. Engineers already design around this danger. Operators of other satellites receive regular warnings and change course when a close approach is predicted.

If the amount of debris in a crowded orbit grows large enough, a single collision can produce thousands of fragments, each of which may strike something else. Under those conditions the number of pieces could keep rising even if every launch stopped tomorrow. Some orbits, Kessler warned, might become too hazardous to use for generations.

original_item.passage:
Ynes Mexia began the work that made her name only at the age of fifty-five. Born in 1870, she spent decades in office jobs that left little room for her restless energy or her love of the outdoors. In her early fifties, while living in San Francisco, she joined a hiking club and enrolled in a botany course at the University of California. Within a few short years she had found her true calling.

Botanists of the time depended on collectors who traveled to remote places, gathered plants, and sent dried, carefully labeled specimens back to museums. The work was physically hard, slow, and often lonely. Mexia took to it with remarkable stamina. On her first major expedition, to western Mexico in 1925, she fell from a cliff and broke several ribs, recovered, and kept collecting. She brought back about fifteen hundred specimens, among them a plant entirely new to science, which was later named in her honor.

Over the following thirteen years she traveled through Mexico, Alaska, Brazil, Peru, and Ecuador. She often hired local guides and traveled by canoe or on foot for weeks at a time. In Brazil she spent months on the upper Amazon, at one point living in a small boat while she pressed and dried her plants on board. By the end of her career she had gathered roughly one hundred fifty thousand specimens, and some five hundred species were new to science.

Mexia kept detailed field notes, recording where each plant grew, what grew beside it, and how the local people used it. Researchers still consult those notes, because a dried leaf in a museum drawer says little about the living plant without them.

She died in 1938, still planning her next trip. Her specimens still fill drawers in herbaria across the world today.
